newsitem.title: FRANCE: Socialist govt fails to clarify N. Caledonia.
newsitem.headline: Socialist govt fails to clarify N. Caledonia.

text.p: France's new Socialist government said on Wednesday it would review the position of state mining company Eramet, which had objected furiously to plans by the previous government to sell nickel mined by Eramet on New Caledonia locally to appease separatists.
Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's office said in a statement that the state would respect the interests of Eramet and its minority shareholders, and Eramet immediately welcomed the news.
"We think it is positive that the government wants to reconsider the whole issue and consult all players involved," an Eramet spokesman said.
Eramet is the world's third largest nickel producer and is 55 percent owned by the French state.

But the conservative government had angered Eramet before being voted out in June by saying it wanted to use nickel from one of Eramet's mines on the Pacific territory of New Caledonia to supply a plant that local company Societe Miniere de Sud Pacifique (SMSP) and Canadian group Falconbridge want to build in the north of the island.
The move was intended to appease local separatists ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence for the island, a French overseas territory.
Jospin's office said, however, that it supported plans to build a new nickel smelter in the north of the overseas territory and ordered a study on its "economic and industrial prospects".
Philippe Essig, a former civil servant and president of state railways operator SNCF, will conduct the study during the summer.

But the management of Eramet, which plans to raise annual production of nickel in New Caledonia by over 6,000 tonnes from its current 54,000 tonnes, made clear they opposed any plans that might limit their expansion.
The board met on Wednesday to discuss proposals from minority shareholders and to decide the composition of a new board that will be presented for approval at the annual general meeting on July 31.
The new board will include three staff representatives and two figures from New Caledonia who will be named soon.
"They will help us better understand issues in New Caledonia," the spokesman said.
Eramet chairman Yves Rambaud, whose position came under threat during the dispute with the state, is now widely expected to keep his post.
Sources close to the issue said the new board was now fairly balanced between company and state officials, employees and independent members.
While the government wanted to give itself more time to review the issue, they said it had already shown it would adopt a less confrontational stance than its predecessor.
"All conditions are there for finding a balanced solution," one source said. "We are entering a whole new logic. The method has changed."
Eramet closed up 1.75 percent at 290 francs.
